sections.overview: The Eurasian red squirrel is a small tree-dwelling rodent widespread across Europe and northern Asia. Curved claws and powerful hind limbs aid climbing and leaping; its long bushy tail helps balance and thermoregulation. It feeds mainly on plant foods that change with forest and season. Usually foraging alone, individuals may share winter nests. Autumn scatter-hoarding stores food and sometimes disperses seeds. The species remains widespread globally, despite sharp regional declines in parts of Britain and Italy.
sections.identification: Adults typically have a 20–25 cm head-and-body length, a 14–24 cm tail and a mass of 200–475 g. Males and females are very similar in external size; seasonal and regional variation affects mass. The consulted references do not provide a reliable standard body width or height. This slender squirrel has prominent eyes, a long bushy tail and, in winter, often tufted ears. Its coat ranges from bright red or chestnut to brown, greyish or nearly black, commonly with a pale underside; the name does not describe every animal. In a Hokkaido subspecies, specimens had lighter winter coats and more pronounced seasonal colour shifts, but appearance also varies geographically. The North American eastern grey squirrel, Sciurus carolinensis, is a different species; colour alone cannot distinguish them because red squirrels may also be grey or dark.
sections.habitat: Red squirrels inhabit boreal conifer forests, mixed and broad-leaved woods, wooded parks and some fragmented landscapes. Local food and tree structure shape their use of habitat: conifer seeds may be dependable, while deciduous woods supply seasonal nuts, buds and fruit. In one northern Greek mixed forest, four adults used the canopy extensively, especially small branches and terminal twigs. This study illustrates how connected crowns provide feeding and escape routes, not a universal habitat preference. Squirrels build twig nests high in trees and line them with softer material; they may also use cavities.
sections.diet: Seeds and nuts are staple foods, but the menu shifts with season and habitat. Cones and seeds may dominate in conifer forest; buds, shoots and flowers become important at other times, supplemented by berries, fungi and deciduous seeds. Incisors strip cone scales and open hard seed coverings. Some animal matter is also eaten, though plants predominate. Rather than one larder, squirrels bury food in many separate caches. In a Japanese Korean-pine forest, researchers documented red squirrels carrying cones and burying seed clusters; those observations describe that population and tree system.
sections.behavior: Curved claws grip bark, letting squirrels climb trunks and move onto slender branches. In northern Greece, clawed climbing aided vertical travel and retreat to trees after ground feeding; quadrupedal movement and sitting helped squirrels use terminal twigs and handle food. Jumps cross gaps between crowns. The long tail helps balance and thermoregulation, while hind limbs support climbing and leaps. Red squirrels forage mostly alone rather than in stable troops. Their home ranges overlap, and familiar individuals may tolerate one another or share nests during cold periods. Space use shifts with food and breeding conditions.
sections.reproduction: Breeding timing varies with latitude, food and condition. Gestation lasts about 38–39 days. When a female is receptive, several males may follow and compete; mating does not establish a lasting pair bond, and males provide no routine care. The female raises the litter in a nest and may move young if disturbed. Newborns are blind and sparsely furred; eyes open at about a month, and young begin leaving the nest at roughly 40–45 days. They sample solid food before weaning at around 8–10 weeks, remaining under maternal care during early life. Litter size and breeding frequency vary, so regional averages are not fixed outputs for the species.
sections.ecology: Scatter-hoarding links squirrel feeding with forest regeneration. In Hokkaido, Japan, red squirrels carried Korean-pine cones from source trees and buried seeds in small clusters. One study found seedlings as far as 600 m from parent trees; another recorded them up to 1.8 km from the nearest source. These are separate site-specific observations, not a typical distance. Squirrels recover some caches; seeds left in suitable microsites may germinate. This interaction is documented for Korean pine in parts of East Asia, not every tree or squirrel population. Caches also provide food when fresh resources are scarce.
sections.conservation: The 2023 IUCN global assessment classifies the species as Least Concern because of its broad Eurasian range; this does not mean all populations are secure. In Britain, introduced eastern grey squirrels compete with red squirrels and can carry squirrelpox virus, which causes severe disease and mortality in reds. English surveillance from 1993–2005 found cases in areas where seropositive greys also occurred, supporting a reservoir link in that setting. Grey squirrels and squirrelpox are not a universal Eurasian threat. Habitat fragmentation, forestry and other local pressures also matter, so conservation needs depend on region.
